title: The Searchers at the Door: Plague in Bombay and Poona
subtitle: Bubonic plague, the Epidemic Diseases Act, the first plague vaccine and the Poona killings, 1896–1898
intro: In August and September 1896 the weekly death returns of Bombay crept above their five-year averages, and fevers with swollen glands were being treated quietly in the crowded grain-dealers' quarter of Mandvi, near the docks. On 23 September a Goan private practitioner, Acácio Gabriel Viegas, said publicly what the returns implied: the disease was bubonic plague, the same illness Alexandre Yersin had isolated in Hong Kong two years before. Within months it had reached Poona, Karachi and much of western India; by the official count it would kill millions across the subcontinent over the next two decades.

The response set colonial power against the household. The Epidemic Diseases Act received the Governor-General's assent on 4 February 1897 and allowed officials to inspect houses, remove the sick to hospitals, hold contacts in segregation camps, search railway passengers and destroy property. In Bombay a Plague Committee under General W. F. Gatacre and in Poona a Special Plague Committee under W. C. Rand of the Indian Civil Service used soldiers, British and Indian, in house-to-house search parties. Officials recorded falling death counts and orderly procedure; the people searched, and the Marathi and Anglo-Indian press that spoke for some of them, recorded intrusion into kitchens and shrines, the exposure of women, burned belongings and families taken to camps. Both positions are given here in their own records. Officials investigating the complaints in 1897 reported them as unsubstantiated; the complainants and their newspapers did not accept that finding.

Fear also emptied the city. According to the Sanitary Commissioner's figures, roughly 400,000 people, a little under half of Bombay's population, had left by the end of January 1897; mills ran a fraction of their machinery, and on 29 October 1896 millworkers stoned the Arthur Road infectious diseases hospital in protest against forced removal. No firsthand account by a millworker has been found for this chapter; they appear in the records of employers, inspectors and newspapers. The same is true of Savitribai Phule, the Poona teacher and reformer who died on 10 March 1897 after nursing plague patients: no surviving firsthand account of her plague work was found.

Medicine moved fast. Waldemar Haffkine, a Russian-born bacteriologist sent from Calcutta, made a killed-culture vaccine in a makeshift laboratory, injected himself on 10 January 1897, and three weeks later inoculated volunteers among the prisoners of the Byculla House of Correction during an outbreak there. The record names none of those prisoners; they survive only as counts. In June 1898, in Karachi, Paul-Louis Simond of the Institut Pasteur showed in a rough experiment that plague passed between rats through their fleas, a finding doubted for years before it was confirmed. An Indian Plague Commission under Thomas Fraser toured India from November 1898 to weigh all of this.

In Poona the measures ended in violence. On 22 June 1897, the night of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee, Rand and Lieutenant Charles Ayerst were shot as they drove back from Government House; Ayerst died at once and Rand on 3 July. The Chapekar brothers were later convicted, and Bal Gangadhar Tilak, editor of the Marathi weekly Kesari, was tried for sedition over articles published a week before the shooting. In London, Gopal Krishna Gokhale's allegations against the soldiers were debated in the House of Commons, and he later withdrew the most serious of them.

Much of the honest record here is administrative: official histories, committee reports, parliamentary answers, a law report, a scientific paper, a photograph album. Two eyes, Gandhi and Damodar Chapekar, wrote later memoirs. Mark Twain, who passed through Bombay in January 1896 and described it in Following the Equator (1897), left before the plague and is not used.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian, as used by the British Indian government and by the English, Marathi and Gujarati press of the period. Kesari and Mahratta were weeklies, so a printed issue date can trail the events it reports by several days.
vantage_key: 0 = principal actor or the person named at the centre of a measure or act; 1 = on the scene in the plague wards, laboratories or searched streets; 2 = same city or province in an official or press role; 3 = elsewhere in India; 4 = in Britain, hearing by cable and post.

eyes.name: Acácio Gabriel Viegas
eyes.role: Goan physician in private practice in Bombay, about 40, with patients among the traders of Mandvi
eyes.where: Mandvi and the municipal offices, Bombay
eyes.vantage_label: the doctor who named the disease
eyes.authenticity: His own report to the Municipal Commissioner has not been located online; its date and substance are recorded in the official history of plague in the Bombay Presidency (September 1896 to June 1899) and in a Bombay Government report naming him to the committee appointed on 29 September 1896. Later biographical accounts are popular and secondary.
eyes.bio: A private practitioner rather than a government officer, Viegas was the first to say publicly that the excess deaths in Mandvi were plague. His statement forced the municipality and the Government of India to act. He then campaigned for slum cleansing and rat destruction and remained a figure in Bombay civic life.

sources.title: Official history of plague in the Bombay Presidency, Sept 1896 – June 1899, ch. I p. 1 (NLS India Papers)
Bombay Government plague report, committee of 29 September 1896 (NLS India Papers)
Acacio Gabriel Viegas (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Brigade-Surgeon Lt-Col. Weir, I.M.S.
eyes.role: Health Officer of the Bombay Municipality, head of its Health Department and of the city's infectious diseases hospital
eyes.vantage_label: the official keeping the city's death returns
eyes.form: official returns and statements (in government reports)
eyes.authenticity: His weekly mortality returns and his comments on them are printed and quoted in the Bombay Government's plague reports of 1896–97, digitised in the National Library of Scotland's India Papers. His forenames were not confirmed.
eyes.bio: Weir's department counted Bombay's dead week by week and ran the hospital to which plague patients were removed. His returns show the excess mortality before the disease was named, and his cautious first reading of them (that migrants from a pilgrimage at Nasik explained much of it) shows how an official could see the numbers and still hesitate over the word plague.

sources.title: Bombay Government plague report, ch. V p. 109: weekly deaths and the Health Officer's comments (NLS)
Bombay Government plague report, p. 9: first cases and Dr Viegas (NLS)

eyes.name: Waldemar Mordecai Wolff Haffkine
eyes.role: Bacteriologist to the Government of India, aged 36; born in Odessa, trained in Paris under Pasteur's school; already known for a cholera vaccine
eyes.side: Government of India medical service (foreign-born scientist)
eyes.where: Plague laboratory at Grant Medical College / J. J. Hospital and Byculla jail, Bombay
eyes.vantage_label: maker and first subject of the vaccine
eyes.authenticity: His 'Remarks on the plague prophylactic fluid' appeared in the British Medical Journal of 12 June 1897 (reprint held by the Wellcome Collection); his retrospective paper on plague inoculation appeared in the Journal of Hygiene in 1915. Accounts of the Byculla trial in official reports differ slightly in their numbers.
eyes.bio: Haffkine was given a corridor and a room and asked to turn medical opinion into bacteriological proof, then to find a preventive. His vaccine of killed plague cultures was tried first on himself and then on prisoners in an infected jail. It became the main anti-plague inoculation in India, and he spent years defending its record against critics.

sources.title: Haffkine, 'Remarks on the plague prophylactic fluid', BMJ 12 June 1897 (Wellcome reprint)
Haffkine, 'Concerning inoculation against plague and pneumonia…', Journal of Hygiene 15 (1915)
Official account of the Byculla House of Correction experiment (NLS)

eyes.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
eyes.role: Barrister, 27, on a visit home from Natal, campaigning for Indians in South Africa

waypoints.label: Poona, meets Tilak and Gokhale, autumn 1896
Sails from Bombay for Durban, late Nov 1896

eyes.vantage_label: in a town waiting for the plague to arrive
eyes.authenticity: Written in Gujarati as weekly instalments in Navajivan, 1925–29, about 30 years after the events; English translation by Mahadev Desai, published 1927–29. Dates in it are approximate. Entries are digests only.
eyes.bio: Gandhi happened to be in India when plague broke out in Bombay and volunteered for Rajkot's sanitation committee, inspecting latrines street by street. His account of finding the rich less cooperative than the poor, and the untouchables' quarters cleaner than many caste houses, is an early record of the sanitary ideas he later made central. He met Tilak and Gokhale in Poona on the same journey.

sources.title: An Autobiography, Part II ch. 25, 'In India' (mkgandhi-sarvodaya.org)

eyes.name: William Forbes Gatacre
eyes.role: Brigadier-General, commanding the Bombay District; chairman of the Bombay Plague Committee from March 1897
eyes.side: British Indian Army and Bombay Government
eyes.vantage_label: soldier placed in charge of a city's health
eyes.authenticity: Report on the bubonic plague in Bombay, 1896–97 (Bombay: Times of India Steam Press, 1897), with volumes of charts and plans; public domain, digitised by the Wellcome Collection from a Royal College of Physicians copy.
eyes.bio: Gatacre ran the Bombay Plague Committee with military methods: search parties, compulsory removal to hospital, segregation camps and disinfection. His report is the committee's own account of what it did and why. Within a year he had left India to command a brigade in the Sudan.

sources.title: Gatacre, Report on the bubonic plague in Bombay, 1896–97 (Wellcome Collection)

eyes.name: Walter Charles Rand
eyes.role: Indian Civil Service officer in the Bombay Presidency, in his thirties; chairman of the Poona Special Plague Committee
eyes.vantage_label: the officer who ran the searches
eyes.authenticity: His report on the Poona operations is printed as an appendix in the official compilation The Plague in India, 1896, 1897 (compiled by R. Nathan, ICS); pages are digitised in the NLS India Papers. Dates for his appointment differ between official pages (10 and 19 February 1897).
eyes.bio: Rand was given emergency powers and a military search force to stamp out plague in Poona. His report claims success in falling death counts and sets out rules meant to restrain the search parties. To many Poona households he became the face of the searches, and he was shot on Jubilee night after the operations had ended.

sources.title: Report on plague in Poona, Rand's estimates and compensation reply (NLS)
Poona Plague Committee and measures before its appointment, p. 89 (NLS)

eyes.name: Charles Henry Benjamin Adams (later Adams-Wylie)
eyes.role: Plague medical officer at the General Plague Hospital, Poona, 1897 – January 1898
eyes.where: General Plague Hospital and segregation camps, Poona
eyes.authenticity: The Getty Research Institute holds 'Poona Plague Pictures, 1897–1908, undated' (accession 96.R.95), about 147 photographs, most likely compiled by Adams; some prints are attributed to the Poona photographer F. B. Stewart. Attribution of the album to Adams is the archive's, not certain.
eyes.bio: Adams worked inside the system the newspapers argued about. His album shows hospital staff, wards, patients, house inspections, segregation and observation camps and funeral grounds: a medical officer's visual record of the measures, made from the side that imposed them.

sources.title: Poona Plague Pictures, Getty Research Institute (finding aid, OAC)

eyes.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
eyes.role: Editor of the Marathi weekly Kesari and the English weekly Mahratta, Poona; member of the Bombay Legislative Council; aged 41
eyes.where: Poona; Bombay High Court for his trial

waypoints.label: Arrested in Bombay, 27 Jul 1897; tried at the High Court, Sep 1897

eyes.vantage_label: editor speaking for the searched city
eyes.authenticity: Kesari issues survive in Pune; the articles charged at his trial are printed in English translation in the law report Queen-Empress v. Bal Gangadhar Tilak (ILR 22 Bombay 112). Kesari is summarised here, not quoted, because only translations are available.
eyes.bio: Tilak's papers carried the complaints of Poona households against the search parties and denounced the officials who directed them. He is the most prominent voice of opposition to the measures and was convicted of exciting disaffection; whether his writing incited the killings was the government's case and remains argued.

sources.title: Queen-Empress v. Bal Gangadhar Tilak: an autopsy (Indian History Collective)
Arvind Datar, The sedition trials of Lokmanya Tilak (Bar & Bench)

eyes.name: Damodar Hari Chapekar
eyes.role: Brahmin of Chinchwad near Poona, about 28, a kirtan performer's son who led a youth club of physical training
eyes.authenticity: An autobiographical account written while he awaited trial and execution, held in official files and published in Marathi as Hutatma Damodar Hari Chapekar yanche atmavrtta (Maharashtra State Board for Literature and Culture, 1974). Contents are given here only in general terms; the text was not consulted directly.
eyes.bio: Damodar Chapekar and his brother Balkrishna shot Rand and Ayerst. His prison narrative presents the killing as retaliation for the searches and for wider grievances, which makes it the only account by an assailant. It was written to justify the act and should be read as such.

sources.title: Hutātmā Dāmodara Hari Cāpekara yāñce ātmavrtta (CRL catalogue)
Chapekar brothers (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
eyes.role: Professor at Fergusson College, Poona, aged 31; a leader of Poona's reformist public bodies; in England to give evidence to the Welby Commission on Indian expenditure
eyes.vantage_label: in England, relaying letters from home
eyes.authenticity: His interview appeared in the Manchester Guardian on 2 July 1897 (date per B. R. Nanda's biography); his apology to the Governor of Bombay was dated 1 August 1897 and announced by telegram on 2 August, as reported to the House of Commons on 5 August.
eyes.bio: Gokhale took to the British press charges against the soldiers in Poona that had reached him by letter. When the Bombay Government demanded proof and his informants would not come forward, he apologised and withdrew the allegation of assaults on women. The episode shaped his reputation for years, praised by some as honourable and attacked by others as a surrender.

sources.title: HC Deb 5 August 1897, Poona outrages (Hansard)
Mainstream Weekly, article on the Poona plague and its politics

eyes.name: Lord George Francis Hamilton
eyes.role: Secretary of State for India in Lord Salisbury's government
eyes.vantage_label: minister answering for India in Parliament
eyes.authenticity: His answers are printed in Hansard (Parliamentary Debates, 4th series, vols 50–52, 1897), freely available online.
eyes.bio: Hamilton answered every question in the Commons about Poona, read out the Bombay Government's rebuttal of the citizens' memorial, and announced Gokhale's retraction. His answers are the official British position in its own words, and they show what London was told.

sources.title: HC Deb 1 July 1897, Outrages at Poona
HC Deb 5 July 1897, Plague in India
HC Deb 5 August 1897, Poona outrages

eyes.name: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata
eyes.side: Bombay Parsi mercantile and millowning community
eyes.authenticity: His statement of 10 May 1897 was reported in the Times of India and his letter of 26 May 1897 is cited from Bombay millowners' records in Aditya Sarkar's study (International Review of Social History, 2014). Not consulted in the original.
eyes.bio: The exodus left Bombay's mills without hands, and wages rose as employers competed for those who remained. Tata's remarks show the plague from the counting house: a labour crisis that, for a time, gave workers bargaining power.

sources.title: Aditya Sarkar, 'The tie that snapped: bubonic plague and mill labour in Bombay, 1896–1898' (IRSH 2014)

eyes.name: Paul-Louis Simond
eyes.role: French naval physician and Institut Pasteur scientist, aged about 39, sent to India to continue Yersin's serum treatment
eyes.authenticity: 'La propagation de la peste' appeared in the Annales de l'Institut Pasteur, vol. 12 (1898). His description of the emotion he felt on 2 June 1898 is a later recollection quoted by the Institut Pasteur. French only; digests here.
eyes.bio: Simond noticed small blisters on plague patients and suspected that rats did not pass the disease to people directly. In Karachi he showed that healthy rats caught plague from sick ones only when fleas could pass between them. The idea was received with doubt and confirmed only some years later.

sources.title: Institut Pasteur, Paul-Louis Simond, le multimissionnaire des maladies
In search of lost fleas: reconsidering Simond's contribution (PMC)

eyes.name: Thomas Richard Fraser
eyes.role: Professor of materia medica at Edinburgh; president of the Indian Plague Commission
eyes.side: British medical establishment; Government of India inquiry
eyes.where: Bombay and other plague centres, then London
eyes.vantage_label: the inquiry that weighed the evidence
eyes.authenticity: Minutes of Evidence taken by the Indian Plague Commission (Calcutta, 1899) and the Commission's Report (1900–01) are government publications in the public domain. Members: Fraser (president), J. P. Hewett, A. E. Wright, A. Cumine, M. A. Ruffer; secretary C. J. Hallifax.
eyes.bio: Fraser's commission questioned officials, physicians and Indian witnesses across India about how plague spread, whether Haffkine's vaccine worked and what the measures had cost. It is the inquiry that closed this chapter, and it re-examined Haffkine's figures more strictly than he had.

sources.title: Minutes of Evidence taken by the Indian Plague Commission, vol. II (NVLI)
Official page listing the Commission's members and its arrival in Bombay (NLS)

entries.headline: Fevers with swollen necks noticed in Mandvi
entries.digest: Early in September the Health Officer's staff noticed cases of fever with swellings of the neck glands in Mandvi, the dockside quarter of grain dealers and warehouses. Some such cases had apparently been treated by Indian practitioners in August without being reported. The cases were watched but not yet called plague.
entries.source_note: Bombay Government plague report, p. 9 (NLS India Papers): Health Officer's account of early September cases in Mandvi. Exact day not given.

entries.headline: Weekly deaths run well above average
entries.digest: The municipal returns showed 613 deaths in the week, against a five-year average of 478 for the same week; the excess had been building since August, mostly under 'fevers' and respiratory illness, while cholera was falling away. Weir warned against reading the excess as plague, noting that much of it fell on people not born in Bombay and linking it to crowds returning from a religious fair at Nasik.
entries.source_note: Bombay Government plague report, ch. V p. 109 (NLS): weekly table and Health Officer's interpretation.

entries.headline: A private doctor says the word: plague
entries.digest: Viegas stated publicly that plague was present in the city and reported it officially to the Municipal Commissioner. The official history dates the recognition of the disease to this day. When the Health Officer was questioned, he answered that the cases Viegas referred to were already receiving serious attention.
entries.source_note: Official history of plague in the Bombay Presidency, Sept 1896 – June 1899, ch. I p. 1 (NLS); Bombay Government report p. 9 (NLS).

entries.headline: Named to the committee on the outbreak
entries.digest: Six days after his statement, the Surgeon-General reported seeing about twenty mild cases of bubonic plague in the affected locality, and a committee of physicians was appointed to examine the outbreak, with Viegas among its members. The same day the Government of India was officially informed.
entries.source_note: Bombay Government plague report (NLS, committee of 29 September 1896); official history ch. I p. 1 (NLS).

entries.headline: 145 plague cases, 89 of them in Mandvi
entries.digest: The municipal returns for the week now counted plague by name: 145 cases, 89 of them in the Mandvi quarter. Once the disease was looked for, it was found to be spread widely through the city, and the later official review concluded that many earlier deaths had been undetected plague.
entries.source_note: Bombay Government plague report, ch. V p. 109 (NLS).

entries.headline: From medical opinion to bacteriological proof
entries.digest: Ordered from Calcutta on 29 September, Haffkine set up a small laboratory in the Grant Medical College buildings. Bacteriological examination confirmed plague in Bombay on 13 October. He then turned to making a preventive from cultures of the plague bacillus killed by heat.
entries.source_note: Official history ch. I p. 1 (NLS) for the dates 29 Sept and 13 Oct; the laboratory's location from Wikipedia's Bombay plague epidemic article. Haffkine's own part in the 13 October confirmation is inferred from the official phrasing.

entries.headline: Inspecting latrines street by street in Rajkot
entries.digest: With panic in Bombay and fear that plague would reach Rajkot, Gandhi offered his services to the state's sanitation work and was put on the committee. It inspected latrines in every street. The poor accepted the inspectors and made the changes asked of them; some wealthy households refused entry and had the filthiest latrines. In the untouchables' quarter, which he had expected to be worst, he found the houses clean.
entries.source_note: An Autobiography, Part II ch. 25 'In India' (Desai translation, 1927–29), written about 30 years later; no exact date given.

entries.headline: In Poona, seeking Tilak's and Gokhale's support
entries.digest: On the same Indian journey Gandhi went to Poona to win support for a public meeting on the grievances of Indians in South Africa, and called on both Tilak and Gokhale. In his memoir he contrasts the two: Tilak vast like the ocean, Gokhale like the Ganges, inviting one to bathe. Plague was then only beginning in western India.
entries.source_note: An Autobiography, Part II, the chapters following 'In India'; the meetings are described there, the date is not fixed. Not re-read for this chapter beyond the Rajkot chapter.

entries.headline: Testing the vaccine on himself
entries.digest: Having found the killed-culture fluid safe in animals, Haffkine injected himself with it to show that it could be given to people. Later accounts say he suffered fever and local soreness but no lasting harm; he used the result to win consent for wider trials.
entries.source_note: Date widely reported in histories of the vaccine (e.g. 'This Day in Jewish History'); his symptoms as summarised in later accounts, not checked against his own text.

entries.headline: Inoculating volunteers among prisoners in an infected jail
entries.digest: Plague had broken out in the Byculla jail on 23 January, and on the afternoon of 30 January inoculation was offered to the inmates; about half volunteered. The record names none of them. Three men inoculated that day were already ill and died that evening, and were left out of the results. Of the rest, 172 uninoculated prisoners had 12 cases and 6 deaths, while the 147 inoculated had 2 cases.
entries.source_note: Official account of the Byculla House of Correction experiment, p. 36 (NLS). Haffkine's 1915 paper gives 154 inoculated of 337 and says both inoculated cases recovered.

entries.date_display: February 1897 (official dates of 10 and 19 February differ)
entries.headline: Put in charge of plague measures in Poona
entries.digest: With plague spreading in Poona and many cases thought to be concealed, Rand was directed to take charge of the measures. A medical officer, Dr Beveridge, had proposed on 25 February organised search parties, fumigators and limewashers, special segregation, and the use of volunteers from the British regiments in Poona. The Epidemic Diseases Act, assented to on 4 February, supplied the legal powers.
entries.source_note: Poona Plague Committee section, p. 89 (NLS) gives 10 February; The Plague in India 1896–97 vol. II app. VI as cited in Mainstream Weekly gives 19 February.

entries.headline: A general takes over Bombay's plague fight
entries.digest: Under the new Act the Bombay Government placed the city's plague operations under a committee chaired by General Gatacre. It organised house-to-house searches, compulsory removal of the sick to hospital, segregation of contacts in camps, disinfection and the burning of infected goods. The committee's own report describes these as the only way to check a disease that families were hiding.
entries.source_note: Gatacre, Report on the bubonic plague in Bombay, 1896–97 (Wellcome catalogue); day of the committee's formation not verified.

entries.headline: Search parties with soldiers begin in Poona
entries.digest: The Special Plague Committee's search operations began, with parties of soldiers, about a third of them British and the rest Indian, entering houses under officers to find the sick and hidden dead. Rand's instructions allowed parties to destroy only the bedding and mats of plague patients, and only in the presence of a medical officer. The operations continued until 19 May.
entries.source_note: Start and end dates from Wikipedia (Chapekar brothers); composition of parties from Hamilton's statement, HC Deb 5 July 1897; rule on bedding from Rand's report (NLS).

entries.headline: Kesari carries the complaints of searched households
entries.digest: Through the weeks of searches Kesari and the Mahratta printed complaints from Poona households: soldiers entering kitchens and shrines, people sent to hospital without proper examination, belongings burned, women exposed to view. Tilak argued that the government's methods were driving people to hide the sick. On 10 May some 2,000 citizens sent a memorial to the Governor setting out such complaints.
entries.source_note: Content of the press complaints as summarised by Hamilton in HC Deb 1 and 5 July 1897 and by the memorial of 10 May; individual Kesari issues not consulted.

entries.headline: Photographing wards, camps and house inspections
entries.digest: Adams's album records the operations from inside: hospital staff in groups, patients in the wards, a forced house inspection, families in segregation and observation camps, and funeral grounds. It is the visual counterpart to Rand's report, made by the side that carried out the measures.
entries.source_note: Getty Research Institute, Poona Plague Pictures (96.R.95), finding aid; individual photographs are not dated in the description.

entries.headline: Following Rand through the weeks of searches
entries.digest: In his prison narrative Damodar Chapekar presents the searches as an outrage against religion and households and says he resolved to kill Rand. Other accounts drawn from the case say he followed Rand for about two months before acting. He wrote this after his arrest, to justify the killing.
entries.source_note: Chapekar's Marathi autobiography (published 1974) as summarised in secondary accounts (CSHC substack; Wikipedia); text not consulted directly.

entries.headline: Millowners in the 'unenviable position of employees'
entries.digest: With much of the workforce gone and mills running a fraction of their machinery, Tata told a meeting reported in the Times of India that daily wages had reversed the usual relation: employers were now the ones bargaining from weakness. The exodus had given millhands a scarcity value.
entries.source_note: Times of India report of 10 May 1897, as cited by Sarkar (IRSH 2014); original not consulted.

entries.headline: Reply on compensation for burned property
entries.digest: As chairman of the Poona Plague Committee, Rand replied to complaints about destroyed property, setting out the committee's practice on compensation. The government's position was that care had been taken and compensation paid; the memorialists said redress was slow or refused.
entries.source_note: Report on plague in Poona, compensation section (NLS), which refers to a reply of 14 May; content of the reply only summarised there.

entries.headline: Counting the dead, and doubting the count
entries.digest: In his report Rand set monthly plague deaths against the totals and estimated the epidemic's toll in the city at 2,901, adding that the estimate was probably an underestimate. He noted that fear of plague was driving people out of Poona even before the house inspections began, and credited the removal of the sick to villages outside the city with lowering mortality.
entries.quote: probably too low rather than too high
entries.source_note: Rand's report, printed in The Plague in India 1896–97 (NLS page).

entries.headline: A proposal to bring in labour from the north
entries.digest: In a letter Tata proposed importing workers from northern India to replace the millhands who had fled, a plan to break the wage rise that scarcity had produced.
entries.source_note: Letter dated 26 May 1897, cited by Sarkar (IRSH 2014).

entries.headline: Haffkine publishes his account of the vaccine
entries.digest: The British Medical Journal printed Haffkine's 'Remarks on the plague prophylactic fluid', setting out how the fluid was made and the first results of inoculation, including the jail experiment. It placed the Bombay trials before the British medical profession.
entries.source_note: Wellcome Collection record of the reprint from BMJ, 12 June 1897, pp. 1461–62.

entries.headline: Shivaji festival report and a poem in Kesari
entries.digest: Kesari printed a report of the Shivaji coronation festival in Poona, including Tilak's speech, which defended Shivaji's killing of Afzal Khan by appeal to the Bhagavad Gita, and a poem titled 'Shivaji's utterances' lamenting the state of the country. These were the articles later charged as seditious.
entries.source_note: Indian History Collective, analysis of the law report ILR 22 Bom 112; ThePrint excerpt of Purandare's Tilak biography.

entries.date_display: 22 June 1897, night of the Diamond Jubilee
entries.headline: Jubilee night: the shots on the Ganeshkhind road
entries.digest: As carriages left the Jubilee reception at Government House, Ganeshkhind, Damodar and his brother Balkrishna shot at Rand's carriage; Lieutenant Charles Ayerst, in the carriage behind, was also shot and died on the spot. Rand was wounded and died at Sassoon Hospital on 3 July. Damodar's prison narrative later described the night as a planned act.
entries.source_note: Dates and outcome from Wikipedia (Chapekar brothers) and HC Deb 5 August 1897; the narrative's account summarised only in general terms.

entries.headline: Commons asks about the press, the memorial and an inquiry
entries.digest: MPs asked whether India would curb the press after the Poona shootings, whether the memorial of 10 May would be laid before the House, and whether an inquiry would be held. Hamilton answered that plague deaths in Poona had fallen from 177 a week to 7, called the vernacular criticism misrepresentation and exaggeration, and refused an inquiry.
entries.source_note: HC Deb 1 July 1897 vol 50, Outrages at Poona (Hansard).

entries.headline: Interview in the Manchester Guardian
entries.digest: Drawing on letters from Poona, Gokhale told the Manchester Guardian that soldiers in the search parties had behaved with grave misconduct, including assaults on women. Published days after the Jubilee night killings, the interview made the Poona measures a British political question.
entries.source_note: Date per B. R. Nanda, Gokhale (1977), p. 110, as cited in Mainstream Weekly; the interview text not consulted.

entries.headline: The Governor's rebuttal read point by point
entries.digest: Hamilton read the reply drafted by Lord Sandhurst, Governor of Bombay, to the Poona memorial. It answered each charge: patients sent to hospital only after examination, one family member left to guard property, lady doctors with the parties, religious feelings to be respected, compensation paid. Balfour refused time for a debate.
entries.quote: In no single case has any serious charge of misconduct been substantiated.
entries.source_note: HC Deb 5 July 1897 vol 50, Plague in India (Hansard).

entries.headline: Arrested for sedition
entries.digest: Tilak was arrested on a charge of sedition under section 124A of the Indian Penal Code for the Kesari articles of 15 June. The government's view was that his writing had prepared the ground for the killings; his supporters saw the arrest as punishment for opposing the plague measures.
entries.source_note: ThePrint excerpt of Purandare's Tilak; ThePrint opinion on the Epidemic Diseases Act.

entries.headline: An unqualified apology to the Governor
entries.digest: Back in India and unable to produce informants willing to stand by their letters, Gokhale wrote to the Governor of Bombay withdrawing the allegation that soldiers had assaulted women, and apologising. A telegram of 2 August told the Governor that the full statement had been posted.
entries.source_note: Letter date per Nanda, Gokhale, as cited in Mainstream Weekly; telegram date per HC Deb 5 August 1897.

entries.headline: Gokhale's retraction and the memorial's signatures
entries.digest: Answering Sir Mancherjee Bhownaggree, Hamilton reported Gokhale's telegram of 2 August. He also gave the result of the Governor's check on the memorial: of 1,699 signatures, 721 examined, only 144 signers found, and 14 of these denied signing; some said they had not known what they signed. The question of extra pensions for the widows of Rand and Ayerst was raised the same day.
entries.source_note: HC Deb 5 August 1897 vol 52, Poona outrages (Hansard).

entries.date_display: 1897 (report published by the Times of India Steam Press)
entries.headline: The Plague Committee's report on its work
entries.digest: Gatacre's report set out the committee's organisation, its hospitals and camps, its searches and its statistics, with volumes of temperature charts, tables and plans of infected streets. It is the committee's case for its methods, written before the Indian Plague Commission weighed them.
entries.source_note: Wellcome Collection record of Gatacre, Report on the bubonic plague in Bombay, 1896–97; month of publication not verified.

entries.headline: Trial opens before Justice Strachey
entries.digest: Tilak's trial began before Justice Arthur Strachey and a jury of six Europeans and three Indians, with the Kesari articles read in translation. Strachey's direction to the jury defined 'disaffection' broadly, as the absence of affection, which became the central legal controversy of the case.
entries.source_note: Indian History Collective (trial sat 8–11 and 13–14 September 1897); Datar, Bar & Bench.

entries.headline: Convicted by six votes to three; eighteen months
entries.digest: After about forty minutes the jury returned a verdict of guilty by six to three, the three Indian jurors dissenting. Strachey accepted the majority and sentenced Tilak to eighteen months' rigorous imprisonment; the printer was acquitted. The Privy Council later refused leave to appeal.
entries.source_note: Indian History Collective and Bar & Bench give the verdict and sentence; the day is the last sitting day of the trial.

entries.headline: Arrested; his statement is recorded
entries.digest: After his arrest, reported in early October, Damodar Chapekar gave a statement admitting the shootings, recorded on 8 October. He was tried, convicted of murder and hanged at Yerawada on 18 April 1898. While in custody he wrote the autobiographical narrative later published in Marathi.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia (Chapekar brothers), citing the statement of 8 October 1897 and a New York Times report of 4 October 1897.

entries.headline: Taking over Yersin's serum work, watching the blisters
entries.digest: Sent by the Institut Pasteur to continue Yersin's treatment of plague patients with serum, Simond noticed small blisters on some patients' skin early in the illness. He began to suspect that the rat did not transmit the disease directly to people, and that an insect might.
entries.source_note: Institut Pasteur page on Simond, which places the serum mission in 1897 and quotes his remark about the rat; month not given.

entries.headline: Leaving plague duty in Poona
entries.digest: Adams's service as plague medical officer at the General Plague Hospital ended in January 1898. The album he probably compiled carries on to 1908, with a later staff portrait among its loose items.
entries.source_note: Getty Research Institute finding aid, Poona Plague Pictures.

entries.headline: Fleas carry plague from rat to rat
entries.digest: In a makeshift experiment in a Karachi hotel room, Simond placed a plague-sick rat carrying fleas in a jar, with a healthy rat in a cage suspended inside so that the two could not touch. The healthy rat caught plague. He concluded that fleas carried the disease between rats and, by inference, to people. Years later he recalled an inexpressible emotion on that day.
entries.source_note: Institut Pasteur page on Simond (date and later recollection); description of the apparatus from standard histories, not his paper.

entries.headline: 'La propagation de la peste' in the Annales
entries.digest: Simond's long paper set out his observations in Bombay, Cutch and Karachi and the flea hypothesis. It was received with doubt: other investigators failed to repeat the experiment, and the role of the rat flea was confirmed only by the Plague Research Commission from 1905.
entries.source_note: Institut Pasteur page (publication in the Annales, 1897–98); confirmation date from general histories; the PMC reappraisal could not be read.

entries.headline: The Indian Plague Commission reaches Bombay
entries.digest: Fraser's commission, with Hewett, Wright, Cumine and Ruffer, arrived in Bombay to begin taking evidence on the origin and spread of plague, the value of inoculation and serum, and the measures used. It went on to hear witnesses across India and later sat in London.
entries.source_note: Official page listing the Commission's members and its arrival (NLS India Papers, p. 25).

entries.headline: Five hundred pages of witnesses
entries.digest: The second volume of the Commission's minutes of evidence, printed in Calcutta, ran to over 500 pages of questions to officials, plague physicians and Indian witnesses. The minutes preserve the arguments over contagion, rats, inoculation and the search system in the words of those who had run or endured them.
entries.source_note: NVLI catalogue entry for Minutes of Evidence taken by the Indian Plague Commission with Appendices, vol. II (1899).

entries.headline: The Commission's verdict on inoculation
entries.digest: The Commission's report accepted that Haffkine's inoculation lowered both the chance of catching plague and the death rate among those who did, while stopping short of full protection. Re-examining the Byculla jail figures more strictly, it counted 7 cases with 2 deaths among the uninoculated against 1 case among the inoculated. It treated the role of rats and their fleas as unsettled.
entries.source_note: Haffkine's 1915 summary of the Commission's reanalysis (Journal of Hygiene); the report's general findings on inoculation and rats from secondary summaries.

entries.headline: Looking back at Byculla eighteen years on
entries.digest: In a long paper on plague inoculation, Haffkine retold the Byculla experiment: 337 prisoners, 154 inoculated, 12 cases and 6 deaths among the rest, 2 cases among the inoculated and both recovered. He set his figures beside the Commission's stricter recount and defended the vaccine's record across India.
entries.source_note: Haffkine, Journal of Hygiene 15 (1915), PDF via Cambridge Core.

convergences.label: The word is said: plague in Mandvi
convergences.note: The private practitioner named the disease; the Health Officer, holding the same death returns, had been explaining the excess by migration from Nasik. The official history credits Viegas with the first public declaration.

convergences.label: Autumn 1896: the laboratory, the returns and a frightened town
convergences.note: Haffkine confirmed the bacillus in Bombay while Weir's returns counted cases street by street; in Rajkot Gandhi was inspecting latrines against a disease that had not yet arrived. Science, statistics and sanitation each answered the same fear.

convergences.label: January–March 1897: vaccine, Act and committees
convergences.note: Within eight weeks Haffkine injected himself and inoculated prisoners, the Epidemic Diseases Act became law, and Rand and Gatacre were given its powers. Inoculation was voluntary; the searches were not.

convergences.label: Spring 1897: the searches in Poona
convergences.note: Rand's report counts deaths and lists restraints on the soldiers; Adams photographs the camps and inspections; Kesari prints the households' complaints; Chapekar, writing later in prison, recalls deciding to kill. The same weeks, four incompatible records.

convergences.label: Mid-May 1897: who bears the cost
convergences.note: As Rand answered complaints about burned property and the Poona citizens' memorial reached the Governor, Tata in Bombay was describing the exodus as a wage problem for employers. Loss was counted in bedding, in rupees and in labour.

convergences.label: Jubilee night and its echoes in London
convergences.note: A week after Kesari's festival articles, the shots on the Ganeshkhind road; within ten days Hamilton was defending the measures in the Commons and Gokhale was accusing the soldiers in the Manchester Guardian.

convergences.label: Late July – early August 1897: arrest and retraction
convergences.note: Tilak was arrested on 27 July; Gokhale apologised on 1–2 August; on 5 August Hamilton read the retraction to the House. The two Poona men took opposite courses under the same pressure.

convergences.label: 1898: the flea and the inquiry
convergences.note: Simond's Karachi experiment pointed to the rat flea months before Fraser's commission reached Bombay to weigh Haffkine's figures. The inquiry stayed unsure about the flea; it would be confirmed only after 1905.

ties.note: Viegas's public statement of 23 September 1896 went past the Health Officer, who was questioned about the cases and said they were already under attention.
Fraser's commission re-examined Haffkine's Byculla figures and reduced them; Haffkine answered its recount in his 1915 paper.
Both worked in plague-stricken Bombay in 1897, Haffkine on a preventive vaccine for the Government of India, Simond on Yersin's curative serum for the Institut Pasteur, where Haffkine had trained.
Tilak's papers attacked the search operations Rand directed and the man himself; the government later held that this writing had prepared the ground for Rand's murder.
Damodar Chapekar shot Rand on 22 June 1897; Rand died of his wounds on 3 July.
The prosecution argued, and some later accounts say, that Tilak's words spurred the Chapekars; Tilak was never charged with the killings, and the extent of any influence is disputed.
Hamilton read Gokhale's telegram of retraction to the House of Commons on 5 August 1897.

Both were Poona men from the same reforming circle around Fergusson College who became leaders of rival moderate and extremist wings; in the summer of 1897 one apologised and the other went to prison.
Gandhi called on Tilak in Poona in the autumn of 1896, by his own later account, to seek support for the South African Indians' cause.
On the same visit Gandhi met Gokhale, who later became his acknowledged political mentor.
Adams served at the General Plague Hospital in Poona during the operations Rand's committee directed.
Gatacre in Bombay and Rand in Poona applied the same Act with the same method of military search parties in the spring of 1897.

threads_out.note: The same disease, caused by the bacillus Yersin isolated in 1894. Simond's 1898 rat-flea finding in Karachi began the explanation of how plague moved, which later shaped how historians interpret the medieval pandemic.

The Bombay measures, house searches, removal of the sick and burning of goods, revived on a vast scale the household quarantine of the London plague, with the same complaints that the cure was harsher than the disease.

Haffkine came to the plague from cholera: his anti-cholera vaccine, tested in India from 1893, was the work that brought him to Bombay. Cholera was falling in the city's returns in September 1896 just as plague rose.
Bombay, which Haffkine's laboratory and the plague measures had made India's public-health centre, was the port where the 1918 influenza first struck India in June 1918.
